sentences.text:
(ORAL)
1. Vide this judgment, I propose to dispose off the appeal filed against the judgment and order on sentence dated 18.01.2017 passed by Ld. Trial Court, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, whereby the appellant CA No. 19/17 Rajesh Juneja was convicted for the offence under Section 16 (1) (a) of PFA Act.
2.
The brief facts of the case as per record are that accused was running an establishment in the name of M/s Shri Balaji Food Products.

On 18.06.2008, Food Inspector Gian Chand alongwith Field Assistant S.N. Jindal and LHA/SDM Sh. B.S. Thakur visited the said establishment and lifted 200 grams of Roasted Namkeen from 6 sealed packets at the premises.
The said sample was divided into three parts and packed as per Rules.
Panchanama was prepared.
One sample was sent for analysis to Public Analyst.
As per the report of Analyst, the article was conforming to the standards, yet the sample was found misbranded being in violation of Rule 32 (b), 32 (I) and 36 (2) (a) of PFA Rules.
The result was prepared on 03.07.2008.
3. Prosecution was launched by Food Inspector by filing complaint dated 09.09.2008 with the court.
Accused was summoned for facing trial.

1

4. Notice of accusation was served upon the accused under Section 2 (ix) (k) of PFA Act read with Rule 32 (b), 32 (I) and 36 (2) (a) of PFA Rules; punishable under Section 16 (1) (a) read with Section 7 of the Act of 1954.

5. After trial, vide judgment dated 18.01.2017, accused was convicted for offence under Section 16 (1)
(a) of PFA Act and vide order dated 18.01.2017, accused was directed to pay a fine of Rs.25,000/
and to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 1 month in default of payment of fine.
6. Arguments heard.
Record perused.
7. The neat question in the present case is whether the declaration on the packet of the Roasted Namkeen (seized in the present case) was violative of Rule 32 (b) (i) and Rule 36 (2) (a) PFA Rules.
8. As per the seizure memo Ex.PW1/B the packaging made the following declaration, vizaviz, best before date: "Best Before within 3 months from the date of packed".
The same was treated as defective declaration.

9. The report of the Public Analyst did not find any adulteration in the food product and therefore,
the next issue was whether the aforesaid declaration and the size of label 25.6% of the size of the packet was violating any Rule or procedure.

10. Up front, counsel for the appellant has relied upon the decision in Ram Babu Rastogi & Ors Vs.
State Through Food Inspector, 2012 (1) FAC 56, wherein the court was ceased with a food product with a label read as follows:
"Best Before within 6 months from date of packaging."

entities.text:
Ram Babu Rastogi & Ors Vs.
State Through Food Inspector, 2012 (1) FAC 56
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
11. The Delhi High Court after referring to Section 32 (ix) of the Act and Rule 32 of the Rules came to a conclusion that the use of the word "within", did not violate the provisions of Act. Para 13 and 14 of the Judgment being relevant and same are reproduced hereinbelow:
13.
The allegations of misbranding against the petitioners were that the sample product declared the label as "Best before within 6 months from date of packaging".

The only grievance of the Department was that the word "within" which stood omitted after 01.09.2001 was added by the petitioners in the label and that made the same as misbranded because of clear violation of Rule 32(i).
Had the grievance been that there was no declaration at all, the things would have to be viewed differently with different observations.
The objective of the declaration of the label was that the purchaser should know at the time of purchase, as to whether the article, which is purchased was capable of being used and till what time.

14. The actual label found at the sample article i.e. "Best before within 6 months from date of packaging" conveyed much more than which was required to be conveyed to the purchasers about Rajesh Juneja vs . The State (D.A.) on 4 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64839166/
2
the genuineness of the product.
Mere use of word "within" as a surplusage would not bring the petitioners under the penal provisions of the Act.
By any means, the purchasers could not be said to have been deceived or misled as regards the character, quantity, quality or date of manufacture and the limit of use of the product.
12. That only leaves me with the issue of size of the label viza viz the size of the packet.
13. I have noticed that the accused had tried to raise a defence under Section 19 (2) of PFA Act.
The Trial Court, however, seems to have rejected the said defence as per the paragraph 35, 36, 37 and 38.

The court held that, firstly, the bill could not be connected with the namkeen seized and secondly, the bill did not contain any warranty in terms of Section 14 (A) read with Rule 12 (A) of PFA Rules.
14.

Neither in the Notice of Accusation dated 04.11.2009 nor in the statement under Section 313 of Cr.PC, it was categorically put to the accused Rajesh Juneja that the accused had given a reply Ex.PW1/H2 accompanied by photocopy of the bill of purchase Mark X1 and Form D VAT 06 Mark X2 showing that the food article has been purchased from M/s Ravi Food Products which bill was signed by the Food Inspector and this fact is also categorically mentioned in the examinationin chief of PW1 Sh. Gian Chand, Food Safety Officer

where he admits that he had received a reply vide Ex.PW1/H2 alongwith photocopy of bill of purchase based on the said bill of purchase (photocopy of Form DVAT 06 letter) sent to VAT office, Ward No. 59 and reply was received from the VAT alongwtih information informing that the article was in fact, sold by M/s Ravi Food Products.
Even Ravi Food Products in response to the letter sent it sent its reply Ex.PW1/I2 alongwith carbon copy of bill of purchase.
PW1 further admitted that he found Rajesh Juneja being proprietor of M/s Balaji Food Products and had purchased the sample commodity from M/s Ravi Food Products.
15. In these circumstances, it is amply clear that, it is the very case of the Department that accused Rajesh Juneja had purchased the articles and produced the bill, which stood duly verified.
Fact admitted need not be proved during trial and this is settled legal proposition.

Once the photocopy of the bill has been admitted by the accused with the Department during investigation and the same was duly verified, the benefit of the statutory defence under Section 19 (2) of PFA Act ought to have been given to the convict/appellant.
The same, however, was not taken into consideration by the Trial Court.
Section 19 (2) of PFA Act reads as follows:

[ ( 2) A vendor shall not be deemed to have committed an offence pertaining to the sale of any adulterated or misbranded article of food if he proves-- (a) that he purchased the article of food-- (i) in a case where a licence is prescribed for the sale thereof, from a duly licensed manufacturer, distributor or dealer,
(ii) in any other case, from any manufacturer, distributor or dealer, with a written warranty in the prescribed form; and Rajesh Juneja vs . The State (D.A.) on 4 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64839166/
3 (b) that the article of food while in his possession was properly stored and that he sold it in the same state as he purchased it.]

16. At this stage, it may be pertinent to refer to the decision in Ramanbhai Shivabhai Prajapati Vs.
State of Gujarat, MANU/GJ/0265/1990 and the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Ganeshmal Jashraj Vs. Government of Gujarat, MANU/SC/0108/1979 and the relevant portion is quoted as follows:
"However, it is not the small retailers who adulterate the articles of food sold by them.

State of Gujarat, MANU/GJ/0265/1990 and

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Yet, it is only the small retailers who are caught by the food inspectors and the investigative machinery of the food department does not for some curious and inexplicable reason turn its attention to the wholesalers and manufacturers.

The small tradesmen who eke out a precarious existence living almost from hand to mouth are sent to jail for selling foodstuff which is often enough not adulterated by them and the wholesalers and manufacturers who really adulterate the foodstuff and fatten themselves on the misery of others escape the arm of the law.

The Food Inspection Department prides itself on its statistics by catching small tradesmen and by its gross indifference and inaction, allows wholesalers and manufacturers to carry on their nefarious activities, untouched and unaffected by the penal law."

17. In the said judgment, it was held that mere existence of a bill or a cash memo was sufficient, even though, it does not contain any further details or warranty in conformity with language used in Section14 of the Act.
Relevant portion is quoted hereinbelow:
In my view, both the courts have committed error in not believing the plea of defence under Section 19(2) of the Act of the petitioneraccused.
The learned Chief Judicial Magistrate insisted for a letter of warranty under Section 14 of the Act.
Section 14 of the Act is reproduced herein below:
"14. Manufacturers, distributors and dealers to give warranty:

No manufacturer of distributor of, or dealer in any article of food shall sell such article to any vendor unless he also gives a warranty in writing in the prescribed form about the nature and quality of such article to the vendor:
Provided that bill, cash memorandum (sic) or invoice in respect of the sale of any article of food given by a manufacturer or distributor of, or dealer in, such article to the vendor thereof shall be deemed to be a warranty given by such manufacturer,
distributor or dealer under this section."
10.
In the instant case, it is proved by defence that the petitioneraccused was servant of Lokmanya Co. Op. Consumers Stores and was getting salary of Rs. 125/ per month.

It is true that the petitioner could not show any letter of warranty to the Food Inspector and had also failed to disclose identity as servant of Lokmanya Co. Op. Consumers Stores on the spot, but that does not deprive his Rajesh Juneja vs . The State (D.A.) on 4 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64839166/
4 right of defence under Section 19(2) of the Act.
As stated above, the petitioneraccused had produced Bill No. 17308 (Exh. 50) wherein it is clearly mentioned as "Anand Amul Pasteurized Standard Milk".

As per the provision to Section 14 of the Act, even bill, cash memo, or invoice is given at the time of sale, a separate warranty is unnecessary and the bill, cash memo or invoice would be deemed to be a warranty even though it does not contain the details as to the nature or quality of the article sold.

So, even if there is no written warranty in the prescribed form, the production of credit bill is sufficient compliance of the law which gives protection from prosecution to the vendor who purchased the articles from distributor, dealer or manufacturer under Section 19(2) of the Act.

When the vendor raises a defence under Section 19(2) of the Act, it implies that the manufacturer, distributor or dealer from whom he had purchased the article had sold him adulterated or misbranded article of food and had given a false warranty and exposes the manufacturer, dealer or distributor to prosecution for offences under Section 16(1) and 16(1C) of the Act Supreme Court has also observed in the case of Amarchandh v. State of Punjab, 1984 (1)
F.A.C 1967 that when there was no written warranty in the prescribed form, the cash memo issued by the manufacturer or dealer to the vendor was held to be a legal and valid warranty.(emphasis supplied)

sentences.text: 18. Further, in my view, the Food Inspector, once he was given a bill, was duty bound to verify the same and take a stand on the same.
However, as noted in the additional evidence of the Food Inspector, he never even mentioned this fact in the noting seeking sanction for the filing of complaint.

The duty of the Food Inspector is noted in R. Venkatkrishnan v. Food Inspector (Hgs.)
Food & Drugs Administration, Pondicherry, AIR 1989 MAD 35, and the same is quoted as follows:
"The scheme of the Act is to reach the person responsible for the sale of adulterated articles in the legal sense of the term.

entities.text:
R. Venkatkrishnan v. Food Inspector (Hgs.)
Food & Drugs Administration, Pondicherry, AIR 1989 MAD 35
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Those who by their mistake, negligence act or conduct prevent the inspection agency to reach the source of the evil may be caught in the net.
In actual practice, the Food Inspector will hold first the person found actually involved in sale.
But he should immediately endeavour through him and through independent investigation to spot the seller in the eye of law and prosecute the latter one.
Earnest effort and sound common sense suffice for the purpose.
If the respective role is not clear to him, it may be open to him to prosecute both, leaving the matter to the Court to decide.

In such a case, his investigation should clearly establish the acts of each one, and the Court should afford opportunity to those who claim to have been selling on behalf of others to establish their case.

There is a tendency among the inspection agency to rest content with striking at the ostensible vendor who execute mechanically the orders of the real vendor and to avoid penetrating up to the source of adulteration.
Such an attitude would not be conducive to the fulfilment of the object of the Act."
(emphasis supplied)

19. At this stage, the examinationinchief of PW1 to the extent relevant, may be referred to:
During investigations

, I sent a Letter to VATO, Ward No. 69 vide Ex. PW1/H and received its reply at portion 'X to X' to the effect that M/s Shri Balaji Food Products was a Proprietorship Concern, having Shri Rajesh Kumar as its Proprietor.

I sent a Rajesh Juneja vs . The State (D.A.) on 4 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/64839166/
5 Letter to M/s Shri Balaji Food Products vide Ex. PW 1/H1 and in response thereto, I received a reply vide Ex. PW1/H2 alongwith photocopy of Bill of Purchase of the sample commodity, which is Mark X1 and photocopy of Form DVAT 06, which is Mark X2.

I sent a Letter to VATO, Ward No. 59 vide Ex. PW1/I and received its reply at portion 'X to X' to the effect that M/s Ravi Food Products was a Proprietorship Concern,
having Shri Ramu Gupta as its Proprietor.

I sent a Letter to Ravi Food Products vide Ex. PW 1/I1 and received its reply vide Ex. PW1/I2 (2 pages) alongwith photocopy of Carbon Copy of Bill of Purchase, which is Mark X 3, photocopy of Voter ICard,
which is Mark X4, photocopy of Sales Tax Registration Certificate (2 pages), which are collectively Mark X5 and photocopy of MCD License, which is Mark X6.
On completion of investigations, it was found that vendor/accused Rajesh was the Proprietor of M/s Shri Balaji Food Products and had purchased the sample commodity from M/s Ravi Food Products.
Accused Ramu Gupta was the Proprietor of Supplier Concern namely M/s Ravi Food Products.
20. In these circumstances, in view of the clear admission made by the witness PW1 in examination in chief, appellant is entitled to the benefit of the defence under Section 19 (2) of PFA Act.
21. In these circumstances, I did not go into the fact that accused is entitled to any benefit by the Department's earlier policy of issuing warning to accused persons in case of misbranding.
Appellant is accordingly acquitted.
